thread.title: AI At The Edge: Apple's Smartphone Leadership - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Mark Hibben
title: AI At The Edge: Apple's Smartphone Leadership - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Rethink Technology business briefs for June 13, 2018.
Apple's ( AAPL ) 2018 Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) offered no new hardware this year but instead focused on new editions of all its major operating system platforms. Although there were many new features for users, much of the focus was on critical software infrastructure in Edge AI that uses machine learning resident on iPhone for tasks such as image recognition, natural language, and augmented reality. While Apple still lags in cloud-hosted AI, Apple is out in front in AI on the smartphone.
Swift Shot AR game demonstration. Source: WWDC Platforms State of the Union .
Leadership in smartphone AI The above statement may come as a surprise, since we've gotten used to Apple being characterized as lagging competitors such as Google ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Amazon ( AMZN ). In terms of cloud-based AI, Siri remains relatively dumb compared to AI assistants such as Alexa or Cortana.
Apple still needs to catch up in this area, but last year, starting at WWDC, Apple jumped out in front in the area of on-device machine learning. This was an area that many didn't see coming. After all, with an always connected device, there was no need to rely on anything but cloud-hosted AI.
Apple's rationale, that on-device AI afforded the user a greater level of privacy and security, may have seemed a little pedantic at the time. Subsequent data sharing scandals have brought the issue of user privacy to the forefront, and have probably worked to Apple's advantage.
Apple's approach was two pronged. On the hardware front, Apple equipped the new A11 Bionic processor with a dedicated neural network accelerator. Not much is known about the Neural Engine except that it accelerates inference operations for an already trained machine learning model.
On the software front, Apple introduced Core ML. Core ML provided a set of APIs for developers to incorporate their own already trained machine learning models directly into their apps so that they would run locally on the iOS device. Core ML is supported across all of Apple's OS platforms, iOS, macOS, tvOS, and watchOS, and is supported by most machine learning frameworks:
Source: WWDC Platforms State of the Union.
In addition, Apple provided a set of pre-built machine learning models called the Vision Framework (image analysis) and Natural Language Framework (speech recognition), since these areas are the most frequently involved in machine learning. Vision and Language are supported in iOS, macOS, and tvOS.
A year ago, the idea of locally hosted AI on a mobile device was still kind of a novelty, but this has changed quickly. Last October, Huawei introduced the Kirin 970 SOC with a hardware Neural Processing Unit. However, it lacked an equivalent set of APIs in Android to take advantage of the hardware.
This deficiency was addressed by Google IO only last month when ML Kit for Android was introduced in beta. This has stimulated comparisons with Core ML, such as this article in Venture Beat . The article concludes that there isn't much difference between the two approaches, but I think this doesn't give Apple enough credit for having been in the lead for about a year. It also overlooks the advantages of Apple's tight hardware/software integration.
WWDC sees Edge AI enhancements in machine learning and augmented reality This year, Apple introduced Core ML 2, which promises faster performance, smaller model sizes, and seamless hardware optimization. Apple also addresses the ability to create and train models on the Mac within the XCode development environment. With Core ML, models had to be developed and trained using external tools, then imported into the app via XCode. This process is somewhat more cumbersome than what Google now offers with ML Kit.
Now, Apple developers can create models and train them from scratch using a new set of APIs called Create ML. Training machine learning models is still a much more computationally intensive activity than using them for inference, so training in Create ML is limited to the Mac.
Apple also has used machine learning techniques to enhance its augmented reality platform, ARKit. ARKit 2 significantly enhances the utility of ARKit with a number of new features. Multiple devices and users can look at the same AR scene. AR scenes now have the property of persistence, so that AR apps can be closed and then reopened to the same scene at a later time.
Apple disclosed that it uses machine learning to infer scene details that are outside of the view of the rear or “world facing” cameras typically used for AR. An example of this was given during the WWDC Platforms State of the Union. The presenter pointed out that lighting sources reflected in the globe shown below were actually inferred by the AI:
AR persistence and the ability for AR objects to be viewed by multiple users also appears to rely heavily on Apple machine learning APIs. ARKit provides the ability to map the user's environment in 3D coordinates so that virtual objects can be realistically located within the environment. Knowledge of where the virtual object is in 3D allows the object to be viewed from a different perspective.
(Insert ARKit3DMapping)
In its developer documentation that explains “How World Tracking Works,” Apple doesn't explicitly say that the capability is AI based:
To create a correspondence between real and virtual spaces, ARKit uses a technique called visual-inertial odometry. This process combines information from the iOS device’s motion sensing hardware with computer vision analysis of the scene visible to the device’s camera. ARKit recognizes notable features in the scene image, tracks differences in the positions of those features across video frames, and compares that information with motion sensing data. The result is a high-precision model of the device’s position and motion.
However, inferring 3D scene data from two dimensional video would be an appropriate application for its image analysis capability. I would be very surprised if Apple isn't doing that.
Localized, on device, machine learning is gaining increasing prominence. The initial rationale of security and privacy would probably not have been enough to justify the development for any company besides Apple.
But it's clear that localized machine learning can be useful for a wide variety of applications, with the advantage being that it reduces cellular network traffic while providing more responsiveness within the application.
Apple's robotics opportunity As I pointed out in my companion piece on AI at the Edge, a significant driver for Edge AI involves what are called “collaborative robots.” These are robots that can safely operate around and interact with people. The self-driving car can be thought of as one example of a collaborative robot.
Because of the need to control movement and actions in real time, as well as the need to process massive amounts of sensor data, collaborative robots inherently tend to be Edge AIs. Especially in the case of autonomous vehicles (AVs), controlling these remotely from a cloud-based AI is impractical.
Apple has had an autonomous vehicle program (usually called Project Titan by the media) for some time, and while it hasn't acknowledged any intention to field an Apple branded car, CEO Tim Cook called the program “the mother of all AI projects” in a Bloomberg interview . He also said, “We're focusing on autonomous systems.”
I continue to believe that Apple is not simply developing AI software for licensing, but intends to apply what it is learning in Project Titan to future Apple products. This could be an Apple Car, but it could also be other types of collaborative robots. Given Apple's focus on consumer products, this would most likely be a robot for home use.
An Apple robot would be able to make use of Apple's mobile processing technology as well as its machine learning software. Gene Munster's Loup Ventures has assessed the market potential of Domestic and Social and Entertainment Robots, and estimates that these represent a TAM of $4.6 billion by 2023.
Not a huge market for Apple, but it may be a way to further mature its technology as it contemplates bigger prizes, such as self-driving cars.
Apple is part of the Rethink Technology portfolio and is rated a buy.
